## What we covered

Fee-for-service against capitation, a single model that holds both, and then
what the real programs look like. Bundled payments, accountable care
organizations, and pay for performance. Quiz at the end.

## Key points

- Last week's model was a fee-for-service model, we just hadn't called it that.
  The physician got paid for every unit of care, which is the definition.
  Traditional Medicare still counts as fee-for-service too, even though it pays
  a fixed amount per inpatient stay, because it pays separately for every stay
  and separately again for every outpatient procedure, visit, and home health
  episode. We do something, we get paid for it.
- Capitation is a fixed amount per person, paid whether or not care happens. If
  the year's care costs less than that, the providers keep the difference. If it
  costs more, they absorb it. Since revenue is fixed, the only way left to raise
  profit is to cut costs, so the incentive runs toward less care.
  Fee-for-service runs the other way for the same reason.
- Both are the same model with different parameter values, and everything turns
  on the sign of $B'(x) - p_{d}$. With no capitated payment and a positive
  margin per unit, marginal benefit ends up below the price you pay, which is
  overtreatment. With a payment per patient and a loss on each unit, marginal
  benefit ends up above price, which is undertreatment. Neither is the better
  system. They're opposite distortions, which is why this is a live policy
  problem rather than a solved one. And capitation doesn't drive care to zero,
  since you have to offer enough benefit to attract patients at all.
- The hybrids are hard for a reason that isn't about spending. Bundled payments
  are meant to buy coordination, the hospital caring which skilled nursing
  facility you get sent to, the physician not reordering an image taken last
  week. But paying for coordination means writing a contract that pays providers
  for care they don't deliver, and when many providers share the savings, each
  one's best move is to let everyone else economize and collect a share anyway.
  That's a free-rider problem. You need a large group so one very sick patient
  doesn't sink the budget, but the larger the group, the weaker any individual's
  reason to change.
- Quality got attached to payment because both distortions can harm patients,
  overtreating to the point of damage or undertreating to the point of damage.
  The readmissions program is purely punitive, so the best outcome is losing
  nothing. Value-based purchasing can reward or punish, and scores you against
  other hospitals on readmissions, mortality, infections, complications, and the
  patient survey. Quality of life isn't measured anywhere in it.

## One clarification

I said early on that we're "close" to a capitated model, and then spent the end
of class explaining why hospitals resist capitation and why the most popular
accountable care track has no downside risk. The second version is the right
one. The U.S. has been experimenting steadily in this direction for twenty
years, and payment is still overwhelmingly fee-for-service with other
arrangements layered on top. Don't leave with the impression that capitation is
nearly here.

## Worth knowing for the exam

Work the in-class problem. The answer keys are on the website with the worksheet
answers, and some version of this model will be on the exam. Expect it in both
directions: given $R$ and the prices, find the physician's $x$; or given a
target $x$, find the $R$ that induces it. The second one is the point of the
whole exercise, since it's how a payer actually moves care up or down.

Don't memorize the optimality condition. Memorize nothing, really. Know the
profit function, take the derivative, and the condition falls out. Jumping
straight to the condition is where mistakes happen, and you end up trying to
hold a dozen equations in your head when there's only ever one problem.

Formula sheets are allowed. There are diminishing returns to how much you cram
onto one, though, and the people with 0.5-point font tend to do worst. A sheet
you built while studying helps. A sheet you built instead of studying doesn't.
